subject: playwright
title: Network mocking
description: route() and fulfill(), glob vs regex matching, HAR replay, and when mocking stops testing anything real.

content.title: Intercept, then decide
content.body: page.route() gives you every matching request before it leaves the browser. From there you can fulfill it with your own response, continue it (optionally with changes), or abort it — which is how you test error states that the backend will not produce on demand.

content.title: A deterministic failure
content.body: Register the route before the navigation that triggers the request, or it has already gone out.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: A mocked response is a copy of the contract, and copies drift. Mock for edge cases and error paths; keep at least one test running against the real API so the drift is caught.

exercises.question: Why does this test still hit the real API?

answers.text: The request fired during goto, before the route was registered
The glob should start with a slash
route() only affects XHR, not fetch

exercises.explanation: Routes apply to requests made after they are installed. Register before navigating, or in a fixture that runs before the test body.

exercises.question: You want the request to reach the server but with an extra header. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: fulfill answers the request yourself and nothing reaches the server; abort kills it. continue forwards it, with optional overrides — spread the existing headers or you drop the rest.

exercises.question: The glob '**/api/orders' also matches '/api/orders?page=2'.
exercises.explanation: Playwright ignores the query string when matching a glob without one. Match on the query explicitly, or use a regex, when different parameters need different responses.

exercises.question: Block analytics so it cannot slow down or destabilise the run. Complete the handler.
exercises.explanation: Blocking third-party beacons and fonts is one of the cheapest stability wins in a suite, and it removes a whole class of network-idle problems.

exercises.question: Two routes match the same URL. Which handler runs?
exercises.explanation: Later routes take precedence, which is what lets a test override a broad route installed by a fixture. route.fallback() passes control down to the earlier handler.

exercises.topic: Mocking away the thing under test
exercises.question: This is a test of the checkout flow. What has gone wrong?

answers.text: Line 2 — fulfill cannot take a json option
Line 1 — mocking every API call means the test proves the fixtures render, not that checkout works
Line 5 — the click needs force: true

exercises.explanation: The payment call is the behaviour under test. Mock the surrounding noise if you must, but leave the endpoint the test is named after alone.

exercises.question: Complete the call that replays a recorded session instead of hand-written fixtures.
exercises.explanation: With update: true it records against the live API and rewrites the file; with false it replays. That makes refreshing the mocks a one-command job rather than hand-editing JSON.

exercises.question: What does this verify?

answers.text: That typing triggered a GET to the search endpoint with the typed query
That the endpoint responded within the timeout

exercises.explanation: waitForRequest inspects what the app sent, which is the right level for debounce and query-building bugs — no assertion about the response is involved.

exercises.question: Playwright · network
exercises.back: Context routes apply to every page and popup in that context
exercises.explanation: Put shared blocking — analytics, fonts, third-party widgets — on the context in a fixture, and keep per-test overrides on the page.

exercises.question: How do you reliably assert that a skeleton is shown while data loads?

answers.text: Delay the route handler, assert the skeleton, then fulfill
Throttle the whole browser with CDP

exercises.explanation: Holding the response inside the handler puts the timing under the test's control: the loading state lasts exactly as long as the test needs it to.

exercises.question: A route handler also intercepts requests made by a service worker.
exercises.explanation: Service-worker traffic bypasses page routes by default. Set serviceWorkers: 'block' in the context when a worker is intercepting the calls you meant to mock.

exercises.question: Why does this fixture call unroute at the end?

answers.text: So the mock cannot leak into later navigations or teardown steps in the same context
Because routes are limited to ten per page
To free memory in the browser
It is required before closing the page

exercises.explanation: Contexts are per test, so the leak is bounded — but teardown that talks to the app would still see the mock, and an explicit unroute documents the intent.
